meeting_header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 38 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Luis Romero (Redwood CSM), Priya Nair (CTO, Atlas), Mark Spencer (SRE), Jenna Ortiz (PM), Samir Rao (Infra)
summary: Discovery focused on Atlas Payments' reliability & incident tolerance needs for LLM inference. Key topics: multi-region routing, fallback policies between hosted/dedicated/private deployments, SLA expectations, data residency and encryption concerns. Agreed next steps: share architecture diagrams, Redwood multi-region/fallback docs, pricing and draft SLA, and plan a 2-week POC to run failover tests.

transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?
[00:06] Priya Nair: Hi, Priya here, CTO at Atlas. We've been evaluating Redwood for inference across card auth and fraud models.
[00:12] Mark Spencer: Mark, SRE lead. We're focused on incident tolerance — need to be sure payments don't go down.
[00:18] Jenna Ortiz: Jenna, PM on the payments routing team.
[00:21] Maya Patel: Maya from Redwood, SE — I'll do the deep-dive on routing and fallback options.
[00:27] Alex Chen: Luis from CS is also on for onboarding notes.
[00:30] Priya Nair: Quick context: we have three primary regions — us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-south-1. Typical traffic is 80% us-east, bursts up to 3x during peak. Our main asks are: sub-100ms p95 for critical auth calls and near-zero error surface during incidents.
[00:48] Mark Spencer: And we have strict PCI-ish constraints, we can't send raw card data outside certain regions, need KMS and audit logs.
[00:56] Alex Chen: Totally. Wanted to start with high-level architecture questions: are you leaning hosted, dedicated, or private?
[01:04] Priya Nair: Ideally dedicated for predictability but need to know how Redwood handles cross-region failures — e.g., if us-east is degraded, how do requests failover to eu-west without breaking PCI and with acceptable latency?
[01:18] Maya Patel: Great question. We have a few levers: 1) region-level routing with preference order + automatic fallback, 2) model-variant fallbacks — smaller quantized model in a secondary region, 3) queueing with graceful degradation where non-critical calls are delayed. For PCI you can pin model evaluation to specific regions and use VPC/private deployment so keys never leave the allowed zones.
[01:40] Mark Spencer: When you say automatic fallback, is that per-request? What's the detection criteria — healthchecks, latency thresholds?
[01:46] Maya Patel: It's rule-based: healthchecks + latency and error budgets. You set SLOs — e.g., if p95 latency exceeds 250ms or error rate > 1% for 2 minutes, traffic can be routed to next region or a cheaper/compatible model variant. There's also circuit-breaker behavior to avoid flapping.
[02:04] Priya Nair: Sounds good, but is that out-of-the-box for Hosted? For Dedicated?
[02:10] Maya Patel: Hosted has the routing managed by Redwood control plane. For Dedicated, you get an orchestrated routing layer inside your reserved pools — we still provide the policy engine and can run control-plane actions via your VPC peering or a private control plane option. For Private on-prem, we provide the same policy engine but the control plane sits in your network.
[02:28] Jenna Ortiz: Do you support active-active across regions or active-passive? We prefer active-active for capacity but we need consistency guarantees.
[02:36] Maya Patel: Active-active is supported. We route based on latency and weights; per-request sticky behavior is optional. For consistency — e.g., KV cache or prompt context — we recommend prefix caching per region and a short TTL, since cross-region KV sync can add latency. For stateful things we can replicate asynchronously, but for auth decisions we design for idempotence so the decision doesn't depend on a global KV sync.
[02:58] Mark Spencer: How about failover time — what's realistic RTO?
[03:03] Maya Patel: For configuration-driven routing to the next region, typical RTO is in the order of 10-30 seconds once thresholds are crossed and circuit breaks. If you're switching to a model variant in the same region it's sub-second for new requests, but cold-starts and cache warmups can add seconds for a large model.
[03:19] Priya Nair: Our target is under 30s for critical flows; we can tolerate some latency increase temporarily but not more than 500ms p95 for auth.
[03:27] Alex Chen: Helpful. On SLAs — Hosted has published uptime and regional SLAs, Dedicated has a stronger SLA with reserved capacity. Maya, can you summarise differences?
[03:36] Maya Patel: Sure — Hosted SLA covers control plane and API availability, typically 99.9% with credits for downtime. Dedicated adds capacity guarantees, lower tail latency targets and a 99.95% SLA for the reserved pools; for Private we negotiate enterprise SLA depending on the package. We'll send the draft SLA; Alex will include it in the followup.
[03:54] Mark Spencer: Credits are fine but for payments we need a plan for 'how do we fail open/closed' — e.g., if models are down do we fail to a cached allow/deny rule or route to a human?
[04:05] Priya Nair: Right — by policy some auths can be risk-tiered and fall back to deterministic rule engines. We'd like Redwood to support a per-route fallback policy to 'rule-engine' or 'secondary-model' or 'reject'.
[04:19] Maya Patel: Absolutely — routing policies are per-route. You can define fallback chains: primary model in us-east -> secondary model (quantized) in eu-west -> route to rule-engine service -> return error. Each hop can have timeouts and rate limits.
[04:33] Jenna Ortiz: Any examples of customers who've done that?
[04:36] Maya Patel: We have a payments fintech that uses a similar chain; they keep an on-prem ruleset so when model latency spikes requests hit the rules for a small percentage. We can share a redacted runbook.
[04:48] Samir Rao: On the encryption front: we need KMS integration and HSM option. Keys must be region scoped.
[04:55] Maya Patel: KMS is supported both cloud-KMS and customer-managed KMS for Dedicated/Private. HSM integrations are available for enterprise packages. Audit logs are configurable with per-request tokens and retention controls.
[05:07] Mark Spencer: How are logs exported? We want S3 or a SIEM integration that doesn't leak PII.
[05:13] Luis Romero: We typically support SSE-S3 to customer buckets, or push to Splunk/Datadog via secure connectors; sensitive payloads can be redacted at ingestion.
[05:22] Priya Nair: Ok. For the POC: we'd like to validate a multi-region failover scenario under load. What's the recommended POC scope?
[05:30] Maya Patel: Two-week POC: 1) baseline latency/throughput in primary region, 2) run a simulated degradation and validate routing to secondary region and check latency and error characteristics, 3) compare hosted vs dedicated behavior if you want to see reserved capacity impact. We'll run a runbook with checkpoints.
[05:47] Alex Chen: Who on your side would own the POC infra?
[05:50] Priya Nair: Samir and Mark. We'll provide traffic profiles and a test harness.
[05:54] Mark Spencer: We'll also want to run PCI scope checks and ensure no cardholder data leaves certain regions during failover — how is that guaranteed?
[06:03] Maya Patel: We can configure region pinning per-route so requests with sensitive attributes are only routed to allowed regions. If a route's allowed regions are unavailable, you can choose to route to rule-engine or fail closed. We'll document the exact config.
[06:16] Priya Nair: What about routing latency when region is far — us-east to ap-south — is that acceptable for auth?
[06:23] Maya Patel: For critical auth where you need low-latency, we suggest a hybrid: keep a small quantized model in each region (lower accuracy but fast), or use a two-step flow: local fast check + async stronger check. The two-step pattern reduces end-user latency and puts correctness checks in the background.
[06:40] Jenna Ortiz: Does Redwood support model quantization profiles and automatic kernel selection?
[06:44] Maya Patel: Yes, Redwood Optimize suggests quantization and kernel choices per workload and we've got verified performance profiles per model. For Dedicated we can push optimized kernels to the reserved pools.
[06:54] Priya Nair: During failover, do you warm caches in the secondary region or is there a cold start hit?
[06:59] Maya Patel: There's typically a cold-start spike for KV caches; we recommend pre-warming by mirroring prefixes for hot keys or using synthetic traffic to keep caches warm during an expected failover window. We can automate warmups as part of the failover runbook.
[07:14] Mark Spencer: Can we set a global kill switch to send traffic to on-prem fallback or pause traffic?
[07:19] Maya Patel: Yes, there are global control-plane toggles: emergency pause, re-route to safe-mode, or a 'maintenance' policy. We also expose APIs to trigger these actions from your runbooks.
[07:31] Priya Nair: About metrics — we'll need token-level cost breakdown and latency histograms per route during the POC.
[07:38] Alex Chen: Redwood Console provides per-route metrics, traces, token cost breakdowns, and sampling of responses. We'll give access to a demo org and sample dashboards.
[07:47] Jenna Ortiz: Can we export raw traces to our observability stack?
[07:50] Maya Patel: Yes; traces can be exported to DataDog, Honeycomb, or your self-hosted system.
[07:56] Mark Spencer: On the SLA credits: how do you measure region-level outages? If only one AZ in us-east is down, does it count?
[08:05] Maya Patel: Our SLA definitions are region-scoped and exclude transient single-AZ issues; they count when the control plane detects region degradation per our thresholds. We'll share the legal SLA language in the draft.
[08:16] Priya Nair: Good. Are there any limits on model switching frequency if we configure aggressive fallbacks?
[08:22] Maya Patel: We have rate limits to prevent flapping; circuit-breaker cooldown periods and max switches per minute to avoid thrash. Those are configurable.
[08:31] Samir Rao: For Dedicated, will we own the GPUs or is it pooled?
[08:35] Maya Patel: Dedicated is a reserved pool allocated to you; you don't own the physical hardware but you have reserved capacity and isolation. For on-prem Private we can ship artifacts to run on your hardware.
[08:44] Priya Nair: If we go Dedicated, can we bring our own models? We have a proprietary ensemble for fraud scoring.
[08:49] Maya Patel: Yes, BYOM is supported. We validate and onboard models into the runtime and give versioning/rollout controls. There is an onboarding checklist for safety and performance.
[08:59] Mark Spencer: What's the expected time to onboard a custom model?
[09:03] Maya Patel: Depends on size; typical 1-2 weeks for a medium ensemble including perf validation. We also do a safety scan and recommend quantization profiles.
[09:13] Priya Nair: We'll need detailed audit logs for all inference calls for compliance. Retention configurable?
[09:19] Luis Romero: Retention windows are configurable as an add-on; we can keep logs for the required period and redact PII automatically.
[09:27] Jenna Ortiz: Back to POC runbook — can we simulate partial region degradation (e.g., 50% packet loss) and see how Redwood reroutes?
[09:34] Maya Patel: Yes — the test harness supports simulated latency, error injections, and throughput throttling. We'll instrument checks and produce a post-mortem template.
[09:45] Priya Nair: We have a question on cost: what's the incremental cost of maintaining small models in each region vs active-passive?
[09:53] Alex Chen: We'll include a cost model in the followup comparing three options: 1) Single primary with weighted routing and cross-region failover (cheapest), 2) Small quantized models in each region (higher cost, lower latency during failover), 3) Dedicated reserved pools per region (highest cost, best tail latency).
[10:11] Mark Spencer: Any hidden bandwidth costs for moving KV or warming caches?
[10:16] Maya Patel: There can be egress and backup costs if you replicate large KV sets; we recommend minimizing replicated state and using prefix mirroring for hot keys. We'll include examples.
[10:27] Jenna Ortiz: For the draft SLA, will you include specifics for failover testing and credits tied to failed failover drills?
[10:34] Alex Chen: We can include service-level objectives and a monthly runbook for failover drills; credits are typically for availability but we can discuss contractual KPIs for recovery time if it's enterprise.
[10:47] Priya Nair: One last technical — how are you handling model variants compatibility? Some of our models expect certain tokenizers and the end-to-end latency changes with quantization.
[10:57] Maya Patel: We maintain model experiment matrices. When you onboard a model, we capture tokenizer, quantization-safe transforms, and compatibility notes. For variant fallback, we map inputs to compatible variants and run validation tests.
[11:10] Mark Spencer: What's the expected increase in false positives when switching to quantized smaller models?
[11:15] Maya Patel: It depends; typically you'll see a small delta in quality — we can run A/B tests in the POC and set alerting for quality regressions. Redwood Optimize will recommend configurations that strike the balance.
[11:28] Priya Nair: Ok, recap — we want Redwood to provide: per-route fallback chains, multi-region routing with active-active support, region pinning for PCI flows, KMS/HSM + audit logs, ability to run POC for failover, and pricing + SLA draft.
[11:45] Alex Chen: Accurate. We'll send the documents and proposed POC dates. Anything else?
[11:50] Jenna Ortiz: Can you also include a sample runbook and a redacted customer example?
[11:55] Maya Patel: Yes — I'll share the runbook, a redacted case study, and the whitepaper on fallback policies.
[12:01] Priya Nair: Great. Thanks everyone.
[12:04] Alex Chen: Thanks — we'll follow up with next steps.
[12:08] [END]
